title: Gambhir Lauds India's 'Ruthlessness' After 3-2 T20I Series Win in New Zealand
excerpt: India sealed the five-match T20I series by winning the first three games — chasing 226, recovering from 70/5, and hunting 199 in 13.2 overs — after arriving in New Zealand with a single practice session.
body:
• India beat New Zealand 3-2 in the five-match T20I series, sealing the series by winning the first three matches in a row.
  • Head coach Gautam Gambhir praised the team's "ruthlessness" in those first three games: chasing 226 in the opener, recovering from 70/5 to chase 188 in the second, and hunting down 199 in 13.2 overs in the third.
  • India arrived in New Zealand on October 20, held one practice session on October 21 and played a day later, at the end of a schedule that included the Asian Games and a five-match series against West Indies.
  • New Zealand won the final match by seven wickets in Hamilton, and the tour now moves to a five-match ODI series starting November 4.

India completed a 3-2 T20I series win in New Zealand, and head coach Gautam Gambhir said the result mattered less to him than how it was achieved. Speaking after the fifth and final match in Hamilton — which New Zealand won by seven wickets, chasing 192 in 18 overs, according to Sportskeeda — Gambhir pointed to the first three fixtures, where India wrapped up the series at the earliest possible opportunity.

"Biggest achievement, apart from winning, is how they've handled the conditions and how ruthless they were in the first three games."

— Gautam Gambhir, India head coach

Three chases that decided the series

The numbers explain his word choice. In the first T20I, New Zealand posted 225 and India chased it down despite a middle-overs wobble, with Shreyas Iyer making a 28-ball 42 and Naman Dhir turning the game with a 15-ball 42, Cricbuzz reported. In the second, chasing 188, India were down to 70/5 before Tilak Varma, Naman Dhir and Nitish Reddy saw the chase through. In the third, India chased 199 in just 13.2 overs.

"Three young boys got us across the line [in the second T20I] and then chasing 199 in 14 overs [13.2]... winning the first game after one practice session. That is what is called ruthlessness," Gambhir said. "We wanted to win the next two as well, but sometimes things don't go in your favour as well."

One practice session, three countries, five weeks

The context makes the start more striking. India had a full-strength squad in Japan for the Asian Games from September 24 to October 3, which they won. They were back playing T20Is against West Indies from October 6, a five-match series that wrapped up on October 17. The team then flew to New Zealand on October 20, practised on October 21 and were in a match a day later, ESPNcricinfo reported. Many of the squad were touring New Zealand for the first time and had to adjust to the conditions, the weather and the dimensions of the grounds.

"If we hadn't won this series, no one would have talked about one practice session," Gambhir said. "That's the reality. It's no secret that in India, people see only results, nothing else." He added that the high-risk, high-reward style India have played for the last two to two-and-a-half years will not change: "We will lose matches — sometimes we will lose one-sided games — and that will happen in future too. But our ideology, our philosophy won't change."

Praise for Iyer, and what comes next

Gambhir also commended captain Shreyas Iyer, who now has three bilateral T20I series wins as captain, for leading a side with an inexperienced bowling attack. "Especially with an inexperienced attack, I think he's done a phenomenal job," he said. He also discussed work with Abhishek Sharma on playing spin, noting that Abhishek has struggled against offspin and that improving against it will make him a better player.

India lost the last two matches of the series after sealing it, a finish Gambhir acknowledged he would have liked to avoid. The tour continues with a five-match ODI series starting November 4, where the same questions — preparation time, conditions, and how the younger players handle them — will be asked again in a longer format.
